title: Antidepressants for depression
description: Antidepressant medication is one of the main treatments for depression and is usually taken for weeks before it helps. Studies scanned people with depression while they looked at emotional faces or pictures, before and after treatment. After treatment, emotional areas such as the amygdala responded less, and areas at the front of the brain that help control attention responded more. In the first part, brightness shows how the brain differed from people without the condition before treatment. In "What changed", brightness shows the change since before treatment: warmer means more than before, violet means less than before.
caveat: The "before" difference comes from one study of 11 people with depression and 11 without. The changes come from a pooled analysis of 9 studies of emotional tasks. A larger and newer pooled analysis of 36 studies, which only counted findings from searches of the whole brain, found no area that changed consistently across all studies; in subgroups it found the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex on both sides and the medial superior frontal gyrus. That analysis mixed resting and task scans, included ketamine, and included people who had not necessarily responded. Most of the other changes drawn here are still debated. Different medicines and tasks were pooled together. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before treatment, the left amygdala responded more than in people without depression, even to faces shown too briefly to be seen consciously.

phases.name: Taking the medication
phases.caption: Weeks of daily medication. The studies did not scan people during this time, so the brain is drawn at rest.

citations.authors: Sheline YI, Barch DM, Donnelly JM, Ollinger JM, Snyder AZ, Mintun MA
citations.title: Increased amygdala response to masked emotional faces in depressed subjects resolves with antidepressant treatment: an fMRI study.
citations.quote: We applied the masked faces paradigm to patients with major depression (n = 11) and matched control subjects (n = 11) during fMRI to compare amygdala activation in response to masked emotional faces before and after antidepressant treatment.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: Compared with before treatment, the amygdala, hippocampus and nearby areas, the insula and the orbitofrontal cortex respond less to emotional pictures, and the outer front of the brain responds more. Only the increases in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and in the medial prefrontal cortex after longer treatment, were found again in subgroups of the larger, newer analysis.

citations.authors: Sheline YI, Barch DM, Donnelly JM, Ollinger JM, Snyder AZ, Mintun MA
citations.title: Increased amygdala response to masked emotional faces in depressed subjects resolves with antidepressant treatment: an fMRI study.
citations.quote: We applied the masked faces paradigm to patients with major depression (n = 11) and matched control subjects (n = 11) during fMRI to compare amygdala activation in response to masked emotional faces before and after antidepressant treatment.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: In the larger analysis, most areas did not change in the same way across studies. Medicines, tasks and people differed, and the studies do not show that these brain changes are what makes people feel better.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Before treatment, the left amygdala responded more than in people without depression, in one study of 11 people. After treatment it responded less, on both sides, in that study and in a pooled analysis of 9 studies. A newer pooled analysis of 36 studies did not find a consistent change here.
